notes.meaning: David knew his life was coming to an end, so he gave Solomon his final instructions in private. This dying charge was separate from the public address he had given earlier before Israel's leaders. A godly parent's final words carry great weight, especially when preparing a child for leadership.

David told Solomon that he was about to die, using the phrase "the way of all the earth" because death comes to every human being. Even the greatest king on earth must face the grave like any ordinary person. David urged his young son to show courage and act like a mature man as he took up the heavy duties of the kingdom.

True royal strength came from obeying God's revealed law given through Moses. David charged Solomon to keep all of the Lord's rules, commands, and teachings so that his reign would succeed. A ruler's real prosperity depends on faithful obedience to God rather than political or military power alone.

God had promised David that his family would continue to rule over Israel if his descendants walked faithfully before Him with wholehearted devotion. David reminded Solomon of this covenant, which was God's sacred agreement with their family. While the coming of the promised Messiah through David's line was guaranteed, the physical kings in Jerusalem had to remain faithful to keep enjoying God's blessing on the throne.

David reminded Solomon of the crimes of Joab, David's military commander. Joab had murdered two army commanders, Abner and Amasa, pretending to greet them peacefully while stabbing them in cold blood. By acting as if he were at war during a time of peace, Joab brought bloodguilt on the kingdom and defiled himself with their blood.

David told Solomon to use his wisdom and make sure Joab did not die peacefully of old age. Joab was a powerful military leader with many loyal troops, so punishing him required careful timing to prevent an uprising. David was calling for legal justice under God's law, which required that murder be punished by death to remove guilt from the land.

In contrast to the punishment due to Joab, David urged Solomon to show loyal kindness to the sons of Barzillai. Barzillai had provided food and shelter for David and his men when David had to flee from his rebellious son Absalom. Giving these sons a place at the royal table was like a royal pension, honoring their family's faithful service.

David warned Solomon to keep watch over Shimei, a man from the tribe of Benjamin who had shouted harsh curses at David when he fled from Absalom. Although David later swore an oath not to execute Shimei when Shimei begged for mercy at the Jordan River, David knew Shimei remained untrustworthy. David kept his personal oath during his lifetime, but he warned that Shimei was still dangerous to the throne.

David advised Solomon not to treat Shimei as an innocent man. David trusted Solomon's wisdom to find the right legal occasion to punish Shimei with death for his treason. David wanted justice done for the kingdom's security without breaking the personal oath he had sworn during his own life.

David passed away and was buried on Mount Zion in the City of David. The phrase "rested with his fathers" meant he joined his ancestors in the realm of the dead after a long life of serving God. His burial place became the traditional tomb site for the kings of Judah.

David reigned as king for a total of forty years. He ruled over the tribe of Judah for seven years in Hebron, and then over all twelve tribes of Israel for thirty-three years in Jerusalem. This round number represents a full, complete generation of godly leadership.

Solomon took the throne as his father's rightful heir, and God firmly established his royal rule. The nation accepted Solomon's leadership, fulfilling God's promise that David's son would succeed him. This secure start laid the foundation for the peace and prosperity of Solomon's kingdom.

Adonijah, David's older son who had recently tried to seize the throne, came to visit Solomon's mother, Bathsheba. Bathsheba asked if he came in peace because she suspected he might still want revenge after his failed coup. Adonijah assured her that his visit was peaceful, though his hidden motives remained dangerous.

Adonijah told Bathsheba that he had an important matter to discuss with her. Bathsheba permitted him to speak so she could hear what he wanted. She listened carefully, knowing the delicate political situation between her son and Adonijah.

Adonijah claimed that the kingdom had rightfully belonged to him as the oldest living son and that all the people had expected him to rule. He then admitted that the kingship had shifted to Solomon because it was the Lord's will. By sounding pious and resigned, Adonijah tried to win Bathsheba's sympathy before making his real request.

Adonijah asked Bathsheba for a single favor and begged her not to turn him away in shame. Bathsheba told him to tell her what he wanted. His humble approach was designed to make his request seem small and harmless.

Adonijah asked Bathsheba to plead with King Solomon to give him Abishag, David's young caregiver, as his wife. In the ancient Near East, taking a deceased king's wife or concubine was often viewed as claiming a right to the royal throne. Though Abishag had remained a virgin, she was legally considered part of David's royal household.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Abishag the Shunammite may be the same person as the Shulamite woman in the Song of Solomon, giving Solomon a personal reason to reject the request.

notes.meaning: Bathsheba agreed to take Adonijah's request to King Solomon. She may have felt pity for Adonijah, or she may have wanted Solomon to see for himself what his older brother was planning. In either case, she promised to act as a messenger on his behalf.

When Bathsheba entered the royal court, Solomon stood up to greet her, bowed with deep respect, and had a throne set for her at his right hand. In ancient Israel, the queen mother held a formal office of great dignity and honor, outranking the king's wives. Sitting at the king's right hand showed that she held the highest place of honor next to the king himself.

Bathsheba told Solomon she had one small request and asked him not to refuse her. Solomon warmly encouraged his mother to ask, promising that he would not deny her if it was right to grant. Bathsheba presented the matter as minor, not realizing or openly revealing how dangerous it truly was.

Bathsheba presented the request, asking that Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah as his wife. She emphasized that Adonijah was Solomon's brother, appealing to family ties. To her, it seemed like a harmless gesture of comfort for an older brother who had lost the throne.

Solomon immediately saw through the plot and answered his mother with sharp irony. He pointed out that since Adonijah was the older brother, asking for the king's concubine was practically the same as asking for the crown itself. By linking Adonijah to his old co-conspirators, Abiathar the priest and Joab the general, Solomon showed he knew the rebellion was still alive.

Solomon made a solemn oath before the Lord that Adonijah would pay for this treasonous scheme with his life. The king recognized that Adonijah had broken the terms of his earlier pardon by continuing to reach for the throne. Solomon knew that securing peace and protecting God's chosen kingdom required swift and decisive justice.
